subject: Medicine
summary: Chest X‑ray is a bedside tool to identify pneumonia, pleural effusion, cardiac enlargement and other acute thoracic pathology, especially where advanced imaging is unavailable.

sections.p: A chest X‑ray is a two‑dimensional radiographic image of the thorax taken in a postero‑anterior (PA) or anteroposterior (AP) view, used to visualise lung fields, pleura, heart and mediastinum.
b: PA view preferred for accurate heart size
AP view common in bedridden patients

sections.p: Radiographic severity is graded by extent of infiltrates, size of effusion, or cardiothoracic ratio (CTR).
b: CTR ≤ 0.5 = normal; > 0.5 suggests enlargement

sections.p: In low‑resource East African settings the common causes of abnormal CXR are:
b: Pneumonia (bacterial, TB, malaria‑related)
Pleural effusion (TB, heart failure, parapneumonic)
Cardiomegaly (rheumatic heart disease, hypertension, pericardial effusion)
Pulmonary embolism (rarely seen directly, may show Westermark sign)
Aspiration or foreign body (air‑trapping, localized collapse)

sections.p: Clinical clues guide interpretation: fever, cough and focal crackles point to pneumonia; dyspnoea with leg swelling suggests heart failure effusion; sudden unilateral wheeze after choking hints at foreign body.
b: Focal consolidation → air bronchograms
Blunted costophrenic angle → fluid
Mediastinal shift away → large effusion; shift toward → collapse

t.b: Is there a radiographic abnormality explaining the patient’s symptoms? → Detects consolidation, effusion, cardiomegaly, pneumothorax
Is a pleural fluid present and is it simple or complex? → Confirms effusion when X‑ray is equivocal, guides thoracentesis
Is cardiac enlargement due to heart failure or pericardial disease? → Supports cardiac cause when CTR is high
Is the infiltrate infectious (TB, bacterial) ? → Directs antimicrobial therapy

t.a: If X‑ray unavailable: bedside lung ultrasound
t.b: Can it identify B‑lines, pleural effusion or pneumothorax? → Provides rapid alternative in low‑resource settings

sections.p: Unrecognised large effusion or tension pneumothorax can cause rapid respiratory collapse; missed pneumonia may progress to empyema; untreated heart failure leads to pulmonary oedema.
b: Mediastinal shift with respiratory distress → tension physiology
Progressive infiltrates despite antibiotics → empyema
CTR > 0.6 with peripheral oedema → decompensated heart failure

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then address the radiographic abnormality.
b: Pneumonia: empiric antibiotics (e.g., amoxicillin‑clavulanate) after local resistance patterns; avoid macrolides if high QT prolongation risk
Cardiomegaly: optimise heart failure regimen (ACE‑I, diuretics, beta‑blocker) and treat underlying valve disease
Foreign body: urgent bronchoscopy; avoid blind suction

sections.p: Repeat CXR 4‑6 weeks after treatment of pneumonia or effusion to ensure resolution; vaccinate against pneumococcus and influenza; control HIV, TB and malaria to reduce pulmonary complications.
b: Smoking cessation to lower chronic lung disease risk
Regular blood pressure monitoring to prevent cardiac enlargement

sections.p: Radiographic patterns can mimic each other.
b: Pleural effusion vs. lobar collapse (both cause opacity; shift direction differentiates)
Cardiomegaly vs. pericardial effusion (CTR high in both; silhouette sign and echo differentiate)
Pulmonary oedema vs. pneumonia (diffuse interstitial lines vs. focal consolidation)

sections.p: Certain conditions mask typical signs on CXR.
b: Supine film may hide effusion (deep sulcus sign instead of blunting)
Obesity can over‑estimate heart size on AP view
Early TB may show normal CXR despite active disease

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden respiratory distress with mediastinal shift
Severe hypoxia not improving with oxygen
Rapidly enlarging pleural effusion causing hemodynamic compromise

faq.q: Why does a large effusion push the mediastinum away?
faq.a: The fluid occupies space and exerts pressure, displacing mediastinal structures to the opposite side.

faq.q: Can a normal chest X‑ray rule out tuberculosis?
faq.a: No; early pulmonary TB may have a normal CXR, so sputum testing is still required if suspicion is high.

exam: A 65‑year‑old with fever, cough and right‑sided dullness on percussion – what is the next radiographic sign you look for and what does it indicate? — Look for blunting of the right costophrenic angle; it suggests a pleural effusion.

A patient’s CXR shows a unilateral white‑out with mediastinal shift to the opposite side – what is the most likely diagnosis and immediate management? — Large pleural effusion; perform urgent thoracentesis if symptomatic.
You see a meniscus‑shaped opacity with the mediastinum shifted toward the opacity – what alternative diagnosis should you consider? — Lung collapse/atelectasis rather than effusion.

In a bedridden child with suspected pneumonia, only an AP film is available – what limitation does this impose on interpretation? — Heart size appears enlarged; cardiothoracic ratio may be falsely high.

A patient with known rheumatic heart disease has a CTR of 0.58 – what does this tell you and what further test is needed? — Suggests cardiac enlargement; obtain an echocardiogram to assess valve function.
Why might a supine chest X‑ray miss a moderate pleural effusion and what sign can still be seen? — Fluid layers posteriorly, producing a deep sulcus sign (hyperlucent lateral costophrenic area).
A smoker over 50 has a new peripheral opacity on CXR – what follow‑up is recommended? — Repeat CXR in 6 weeks to exclude underlying malignancy.

What radiographic feature distinguishes pulmonary oedema from pneumonia? — Diffuse bilateral interstitial Kerley B lines and perihilar ‘bat‑wing’ pattern versus focal consolidation with air bronchograms.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: Focused history and a step‑wise physical exam allow you to narrow the differential before the chest X‑ray is even taken.
b: Onset, duration and progression of cough, dyspnoea, chest pain, fever or night sweats
Recent travel, exposure to TB, livestock, birds or asbestos
HIV status, diabetes, pregnancy, malnutrition, alcohol use
Medication history – especially antibiotics, diuretics, anticoagulants
Vaccination history – pneumococcal, influenza, COVID‑19
Occupational exposure – silica, coal, stone cutting
Recent immobilisation, surgery or leg swelling suggesting DVT

t.b: Look for chest wall asymmetry, use of accessory muscles, cyanosis, clubbing; a positive finding suggests chronic lung disease or hypoxaemia but cannot quantify severity
Palpate mid‑clavicular line; increased fremitus indicates consolidation, decreased suggests pleural effusion or pneumothorax; cannot differentiate cause of consolidation
Dullness over lung fields suggests fluid or consolidation; hyperresonance suggests air‑filled space; cannot distinguish fluid from solid mass
Crackles (rales) point to pneumonia or pulmonary oedema; bronchial breath sounds suggest consolidation; absent breath sounds suggest large effusion or pneumothorax; cannot assess size of effusion
Patient sits, percusses flanks; dullness shifts to dependent side indicating free pleural fluid; cannot quantify exact volume
E‑to‑A change over consolidation; positive egophony supports pneumonia; not present in simple effusion

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: In low‑resource settings the chest X‑ray is central, but complementary tests refine the diagnosis and guide management.
b: Chest X‑ray (PA preferred, AP if supine) – assess infiltrates, effusion, cardiothoracic ratio, mediastinal shift; meniscus sign with shift AWAY from fluid indicates large pleural effusion
Ultrasound of thorax – bedside detection of fluid, loculations, and guidance for thoracentesis; absence of lung sliding suggests pneumothorax
Full blood count – neutrophilia supports bacterial pneumonia; lymphocytosis may suggest TB or atypical infection
C‑reactive protein – elevated in bacterial infection; low in viral or TB but not definitive
Sputum microscopy and GeneXpert – detects Mycobacterium tuberculosis; positive result confirms TB
Serum electrolytes, urea, creatinine – assess renal function before diuretics or contrast
Arterial blood gas – PaO2/FiO2 ratio; <300 mmHg indicates moderate hypoxaemia; guide oxygen therapy
D‑dimer (age‑adjusted) – if > (age×10) ng/mL in patients >50 y with low pre‑test probability, proceed to CT pulmonary angiography; otherwise rule out PE
ECG – right‑axis deviation, S1Q3T3 pattern may suggest PE but not diagnostic
Echocardiography – assess cardiac size, function, pericardial effusion; EF <40 % supports heart failure as cause of cardiomegaly

t.b: Question: What is the radiographic pattern? Read: Consolidation = homogeneous opacity with air bronchograms; Effusion = meniscus sign, blunted costophrenic angle, mediastinal shift AWAY; Cardiomegaly = CTR >0.5; Pneumothorax = absent lung markings peripherally, visceral pleural line
Question: Is there pleural fluid? Read: Anechoic space >1 cm depth confirms effusion; septations suggest empyema; absent sliding sign confirms pneumothorax
Question: Is PE likely? Read: Calculate age×10 ng/mL; if result ≤ cutoff, PE unlikely; if > cutoff, obtain CT‑PA; if CT unavailable, consider V/Q scan or bedside echo
Question: Is TB present? Read: Positive MTB signal confirms TB; rifampicin resistance detected if present; if unavailable, use sputum smear and clinical picture

sections.p: Classification systems translate radiographic and clinical data into actionable stages for common chest‑X‑ray pathologies encountered in East Africa.
b: Pneumonia – WHO severity: no danger signs (outpatient), one danger sign (inpatient), ≥2 danger signs or severe respiratory distress (ICU)

Pleural effusion – Light’s criteria (if thoracentesis possible): exudate if pleural/serum protein >0.5 or LDH >0.6; size grading: small <10 % hemithorax, moderate 10‑30 %, large >30 % or mediastinal shift

t.b: CTR 0.5‑0.55 mild, 0.55‑0.6 moderate, >0.6 severe; correlate with NYHA class and need for diuretics
Score each lung 0‑4 based on alveolar infiltrates; total 0‑8; >4 indicates severe oedema requiring aggressive diuresis

sections.p: Several diseases mimic each other on a chest X‑ray; systematic comparison prevents misdiagnosis.
b: Pleural effusion vs. massive consolidation – both cause opacity; effusion shows meniscus sign and loss of peripheral markings, shift AWAY; consolidation shows air bronchograms, no shift

Cardiomegaly vs. pericardial effusion – both enlarge silhouette; pericardial effusion gives ‘water‑bottle’ shape, sharp cardiac borders, may have pulsus paradoxus; cardiomegaly shows smooth enlargement, CTR >0.5

Pulmonary TB vs. lung cancer – upper‑lobe cavitary lesion; TB often thin wall, irregular margins, associated lymphadenopathy; cancer tends to have thicker wall, mass effect, may have hilar enlargement

t.b: Points to effusion: blunted costophrenic angle, meniscus sign, mediastinal shift AWAY; Points to consolidation: air bronchograms, preserved lung markings, no shift

Points to cardiomegaly: CTR >0.5, smooth cardiac silhouette, pulmonary venous congestion; Points to pericardial effusion: globular ‘water‑bottle’ silhouette, clear lung fields, possible electrical alternans on ECG

sections.p: A systematic ladder ensures the most urgent problems are addressed first, then definitive therapy, monitoring, and timely escalation or referral.
b: 2. Identify the radiographic abnormality that explains the clinical picture (e.g., large effusion, consolidation, cardiomegaly).
3. Initiate empiric therapy based on the most likely cause: pneumonia → β‑lactam ± macrolide; heart failure → loop diuretic, ACE‑I, β‑blocker; empyema → chest tube drainage plus antibiotics.
4. Obtain targeted investigations (sputum microscopy, Gene‑Xpert, ECG, BNP, renal function) to confirm aetiology and guide definitive drugs.
5. Monitor response: clinical (fever, dyspnoea, urine output), radiographic (repeat CXR 4‑6 weeks for pneumonia/effusion), and laboratory (CRP, electrolytes).
6. Escalate if no improvement in 48‑72 h, if respiratory distress worsens, or if new signs appear (e.g., mediastinal shift, hypotension).
7. Refer to higher‑level centre for thoracentesis, video‑assisted thoracoscopy, or intensive care when large tension physiology, massive effusion, or refractory heart failure is present.

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Awareness of common adverse effects and interactions prevents harm and allows rapid correction.
b: β‑lactam antibiotics – may cause rash or diarrhoea; stop if severe allergic reaction, switch to a non‑β‑lactam.
Macrolides – risk of QT prolongation; avoid with known arrhythmia or concurrent fluoroquinolones.
Loop diuretics – can cause hypokalaemia and renal impairment; monitor electrolytes and renal function, replace potassium if low.
ACE inhibitors – may cause cough or angio‑edema; discontinue if angio‑edema develops, consider ARB.
Spironolactone – hyperkalaemia risk, especially with renal failure; check potassium, avoid if eGFR <30 mL/min.
Corticosteroids (for severe asthma or COPD exacerbation) – hyperglycaemia, infection risk; monitor glucose and watch for secondary infection.

sections.p: Recognise early signs of deterioration to trigger higher‑level care.
b: Progressive dyspnoea with rising respiratory rate >30/min and use of accessory muscles – consider tension pneumothorax or large effusion; urgent decompression or thoracentesis.
New hypotension (SBP <90 mmHg) with mediastinal shift – suggests tension physiology; immediate needle thoracostomy.
Persistent fever >48 h despite appropriate antibiotics – evaluate for empyema, resistant organism, or TB; obtain pleural fluid analysis.
Worsening oedema, rising BNP, and CTR >0.6 after diuretics – consider refractory heart failure; arrange transfer for inotropic support.
Development of haemoptysis with cavitary lesion – rule out TB or necrotising infection; arrange bronchoscopy and possible isolation.

sections.p: Co‑morbidities and contextual factors modify presentation, investigations and treatment choices.
b: HIV – higher risk of TB, atypical pneumonia, and opportunistic infections; obtain Gene‑Xpert and consider broader antimicrobial coverage.
Malnutrition – blunted fever and leukocytosis; use clinical judgment and lower threshold for imaging repeat.
Pregnancy – avoid ionising radiation when possible; use AP supine film only if essential, shield abdomen, and prefer ultrasound for effusion.
Diabetes – predisposes to severe bacterial pneumonia and fungal infection; monitor glucose closely when steroids are used.
Alcohol abuse – risk of aspiration pneumonia; consider anaerobic coverage and assess liver function before hepatotoxic drugs.
Renal failure – limit nephrotoxic antibiotics, adjust diuretic dosing, avoid contrast CT unless essential.
Liver failure – avoid acetaminophen overdose, adjust dosing of drugs metabolised hepatically, monitor coagulation.
Extreme ages – infants have higher heart rates and different normal CTR; elderly may have reduced cough reflex and atypical presentations.

sections.p: Tailor assessment and management to the physiological and resource constraints of each population.
b: Children – use age‑appropriate CXR positioning; look for primary TB hilar lymphadenopathy; dosing of antibiotics follows weight‑based guidelines; avoid radiation excess.
Pregnant women – prioritize bedside ultrasound for effusion; give β‑lactam antibiotics (penicillins, cephalosporins) which are safe; avoid tetracyclines and fluoroquinolones.
Elderly – expect co‑existing cardiac enlargement; start low‑dose diuretics cautiously; watch for delirium with hypoxia.
People with HIV – screen for TB with sputum Gene‑Xpert regardless of CXR; consider prophylactic cotrimoxazole; monitor for drug‑drug interactions with antiretrovirals.

Low‑resource settings – when CXR unavailable, rely on clinical signs (dullness, egophony, crackles) and bedside ultrasound; use WHO‑recommended antibiotic regimens; arrange referral for thoracentesis if large effusion suspected.

facts: CTR ≤ 0.5 normal; >0.5 suggests cardiomegaly; >0.6 strongly indicates pathology.
Age‑adjusted D‑dimer cut‑off = age × 10 ng/mL for patients >50 yr.
Target SpO2 ≥ 90% (≥88‑92% in COPD) for hypoxaemia management.
Meniscus‑shaped opacity with blunted costophrenic angle indicates pleural effusion; large effusion shifts mediastinum AWAY.
Air bronchograms within a homogeneous opacity point to consolidation (pneumonia).
Four to six anterior ribs visible above diaphragm confirms adequate inspiratory effort.
In supine CXR, fluid layers posteriorly; the “fluid level” or “costophrenic angle obliteration” may still be seen.
Empyema suggested by persistent loculated fluid with split pleura sign on CT after failed antibiotics.

mnemonics.t: Rifampicin, Isoniazid, Pyrazinamide, Ethambutol – first‑line TB regimen.
Vascular, Infectious, Neoplastic, Degenerative, Iatrogenic, Congenital, Autoimmune, Trauma, Endocrine – systematic differential for CXR abnormalities.

vivas.q: Define the cardiothoracic ratio and its clinical significance.
vivas.a: CTR is the maximal horizontal cardiac diameter divided by maximal thoracic diameter on a PA film; ≤0.5 is normal, >0.5 suggests enlargement, >0.6 indicates likely heart failure or pericardial disease.

vivas.q: What is the next step after a normal AP chest X‑ray in a young adult with suspected pulmonary embolism?
vivas.a: Proceed to a CT pulmonary angiogram if D‑dimer is elevated (age‑adjusted) or use bedside ultrasound for right‑heart strain when CT unavailable.

vivas.q: Explain why a large pleural effusion shifts the mediastinum away from the side of the fluid.
vivas.a: The accumulating fluid exerts pressure, pushing the lung and mediastinal structures toward the opposite hemithorax; this is a key sign distinguishing effusion from collapse.

vivas.q: How does an AP film in a bedridden child limit interpretation of heart size?
vivas.a: AP projection magnifies the heart, overestimates CTR, and may hide posterior effusions; PA film is preferred for accurate size assessment.

vivas.q: A 67‑year‑old man with chronic cough shows left upper lobe changes. Which anatomical feature is unique to the left upper lobe?
vivas.a: The left upper lobe has the lingula, a tongue‑like extension of the upper lobe that corresponds to the right middle lobe.

vivas.q: A 25‑year‑old woman with sudden dyspnoea, pleuritic pain and normal CXR – what is the most appropriate next diagnostic step?
vivas.a: Obtain a CT pulmonary angiogram after confirming an elevated age‑adjusted D‑dimer; if CT unavailable, perform a ventilation‑perfusion scan.

vivas.q: Describe the radiographic appearance of silicosis in a stone cutter.
vivas.a: Multiple small rounded opacities in upper zones with eggshell calcification of hilar lymph nodes; indicates chronic silica exposure.

vivas.q: What condition is suggested by diffuse ground‑glass opacities after hay exposure and BAL lymphocytosis?
vivas.a: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis (farmer’s lung) – immune‑mediated reaction to inhaled organic antigens.

vivas.q: How is a positive tuberculin test with normal CXR and no symptoms classified?
vivas.a: Latent tuberculosis infection – requires treatment to prevent progression.

vivas.q: Which CXR finding is most consistent with primary TB in a 3‑year‑old child?
vivas.a: Hilar or mediastinal lymphadenopathy with possible segmental collapse (Ghon focus) and over‑inflated lung fields.

vivas.q: A cavitary lesion with air‑fluid level in the right upper lobe – likely etiology?
vivas.a: Tuberculous cavity with secondary infection (empyema) or lung abscess; in TB‑endemic areas, TB is most likely.

vivas.q: What technical quality does counting five to six anterior ribs above the diaphragm verify?
vivas.a: Adequate inspiratory effort (≥90% maximal inspiration) ensuring sufficient lung expansion for interpretation.

vivas.q: List the steps to assess image quality before interpreting a chest X‑ray.
vivas.a: Check patient identification, film orientation, exposure (no over‑/under‑penetration), inspiratory depth (≥5 ribs), rotation (spine central), and presence of artefacts.

vivas.q: Differentiate consolidation from lung collapse on CXR.
vivas.a: Consolidation shows homogeneous opacity with air bronchograms; collapse shows volume loss, tracheal shift toward the opacity, and elevation of the diaphragm.

vivas.q: Key radiographic signs of pleural effusion.
vivas.a: Blunted costophrenic angle, meniscus sign, loss of peripheral lung markings, mediastinal shift away if large, and possible fluid level in supine film.

vivas.q: Outline the ABCDE systematic approach to chest X‑ray interpretation.
vivas.a: A‑Airways (trachea, carina), B‑Breast shadow, C‑Cardiac silhouette/CTR, D‑Diaphragm (position, costophrenic angles), E‑Edges/Extrathoracic structures (ribs, clavicles, soft tissues). Each step narrows differential.

mcqs.q: A 70‑year‑old with known heart failure presents with dyspnoea. CXR shows CTR 0.62, bilateral Kerley B lines, and blunted costophrenic angles. What is the most likely primary diagnosis?
mcqs.e: CTR >0.6, Kerley B lines and bilateral blunting are classic for pulmonary oedema from heart failure.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT a typical feature of tuberculosis on a PA chest X‑ray?
mcqs.e: Eggshell calcification is characteristic of silicosis, not TB.

mcqs.q: A patient with COPD has an SpO2 of 89% on room air. What is the appropriate oxygen target?
mcqs.e: COPD patients are targeted to 88‑92% to avoid CO₂ retention.

mcqs.q: Which bedside test can reliably differentiate pleural effusion from lung consolidation?
mcqs.e: Physical exam cannot definitively distinguish; imaging is needed.

mcqs.q: A 45‑year‑old stone cutter’s CXR shows upper‑zone nodules and eggshell hilar calcification. Which occupational disease is most likely?
mcqs.e: Eggshell calcification of hilar nodes with upper‑zone nodules is classic silicosis.

cases.v: A 58‑year‑old man with known rheumatic heart disease presents with worsening dyspnoea, peripheral oedema and orthopnoea. CXR (PA) shows CTR 0.58, bilateral pleural effusions, and Kerley B lines.

qs.q: What is the most likely primary pathology?
qs.a: Decompensated left‑sided heart failure with secondary pleural effusions.

qs.q: What radiographic feature helps differentiate the effusions from pulmonary oedema?
qs.a: Blunted costophrenic angles with meniscus sign indicate effusion; Kerley B lines and perihilar haze suggest interstitial oedema.

cases.v: A 22‑year‑old woman presents with sudden pleuritic chest pain, dyspnoea, and unilateral leg swelling. CXR (AP) is normal. D‑dimer is 620 ng/mL (age‑adjusted cut‑off 440 ng/mL).

qs.q: What is the next diagnostic investigation?
qs.a: CT pulmonary angiography to confirm or exclude pulmonary embolism.

qs.q: If CT is unavailable, what alternative test can be used?
qs.a: Ventilation‑perfusion (V/Q) scan, interpreting mismatched defects as suggestive of PE.

qs.q: Which bedside finding would support the diagnosis of PE?
qs.a: Tachycardia with a clear chest, pleural rub, and possible right‑sided pleural effusion; however, physical signs are often non‑specific.

mistakes: Confusing mediastinal shift toward a large pleural effusion; it actually shifts away.
Using an AP film to assess heart size without noting magnification error.
Assuming a normal D‑dimer excludes PE in low‑pretest probability without age adjustment.
Relying on air bronchograms to diagnose effusion; they indicate consolidation.
Counting fewer than five anterior ribs and still declaring adequate inspiration.
Prescribing macrolides for community‑acquired pneumonia in areas with high macrolide resistance.
Missing a small posterior effusion on supine film because the fluid layers posteriorly.
Interpreting a blunted costophrenic angle as collapse rather than effusion.
